---
title: "Single-cell data"
description: >
  Heatmaps, dot plots and markers straight from SingleCellExperiment, Seurat,
  flowFrame and sparse matrices: features by name, groups and annotations from
  metadata, downsampling, sparse summaries, marker ranking, cytometry and
  trajectories.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  message = FALSE,
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 6,
  out.width = "100%",
  fig.align = "center"
)
```

**HeatmapR** reads single-cell data where it lives: `SingleCellExperiment` and `SummarizedExperiment` objects, `Seurat` objects, `flowFrame` and `flowSet` objects, and sparse matrices, in memory or on disk (DelayedArray, HDF5Array and BPCells), as well as matrices and data frames. Features are chosen by name, groups and annotations come from the cells' metadata, and only the chosen features of the cells shown are ever made dense, so a few markers of a million cells need little memory. Five arguments do most of the work, in `heat_map()`, `heat_map_summarise()` and `heat_map_dot()`:

| Argument | What it does |
|---|---|
| `features` | the genes, proteins or markers to show, by name (or a named list of groups of them) |
| `assay` | which values: an assay of a `SingleCellExperiment`, an assay or layer of a `Seurat` object |
| `group_by` | a metadata column (or vector) grouping the cells, e.g. clusters or cell types; several columns for their combinations, e.g. cell type and condition |
| `group_max` | the most cells to show from each group, so small groups stay visible |
| `annotation_by` | metadata columns drawn as annotation tracks |

Cells are rows and features columns, as in scanpy and cytometry data; `swap_axes = TRUE` gives Seurat's genes-as-rows layout.

```{r}
library(HeatmapR)
```

## Example data

A simulated experiment from `heat_map_example()`: 3,000 peripheral blood cells of six types from four donors in two conditions, with 2,000 genes, four of them markers of each cell type. As a `SingleCellExperiment`, the counts and log-normalised counts (`logcounts`) are sparse matrices with genes as rows and cells as columns, the cells' metadata is in `colData()` and the markers of each type are in `metadata()`. `heat_map_example()` without `class` gives the same cells as a data frame, one row per cell, which every function here reads too.

```{r data}
library(SingleCellExperiment)
sce <- heat_map_example("rna", class = "SingleCellExperiment")
sce
markers <- metadata(sce)$markers
markers
head(colData(sce))
```

## A heatmap of cells

`features` chooses the genes (matched to row names, or to gene symbols in `rowData()` when the row names are IDs), `group_by` groups the cells by a column of `colData()`, and the groups are separated and labelled in the order of their levels. `logcounts` is used by default (then `"exprs"`, then the first assay).

```{r cells, fig.alt = "Heatmap of 3,000 simulated cells by 24 marker genes, the cells grouped by cell type into six labelled blocks, each with its four marker genes high."}
heat_map(
  sce,
  features = unlist(markers),
  group_by = "cell_type",
  axis_text_y = NA,
  title = "Marker genes in 3,000 cells"
)
```

Only the 24 chosen genes of the cells shown are read from the sparse matrix, in compiled code; the other 1,976 genes are never touched. A missing feature is an error that names it, and a message warns when the dense values would take more than 1 GB.

### Downsampling and annotations

Large groups crowd out small ones. `group_max` keeps at most that many cells of each group, drawn with a fixed seed by `heat_map_downsample()`, and every cell of smaller groups. `annotation_by` draws metadata columns as tracks beside the cells.

```{r downsample, fig.alt = "Heatmap of at most 100 cells of each of the six cell types by 24 marker genes, grouped and labelled by cell type, with annotation tracks for sample and condition on the right."}
heat_map(
  sce,
  features = unlist(markers),
  group_by = "cell_type",
  group_max = 100,
  annotation_by = c("sample", "condition"),
  axis_text_y = NA,
  title = "At most 100 cells of each type"
)
```

```{r downsample-counts}
keep <- heat_map_downsample(sce$cell_type, n = 100)
table(sce$cell_type[keep])
```

### Genes as rows

`swap_axes = TRUE` draws genes as rows and cells as columns, as Seurat's `DoHeatmap()` does, with the groups and annotations along the top. A named list of features groups the genes too.

```{r swap, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Heatmap with 24 marker genes as rows, grouped and labelled by the cell type they mark, and cells as columns, grouped by cell type along the top, at most 100 cells of each type; the high values form a block diagonal."}
heat_map(
  sce,
  features = markers,
  group_by = "cell_type",
  group_max = 100,
  swap_axes = TRUE,
  axis_text_x = NA,
  title = "Genes as rows"
)
```

### Seurat objects

A `Seurat` object is read the same way, from its default assay's `"data"` layer (or the assay or layer given to `assay`, e.g. `"counts"`, `"scale.data"` or `c("ADT", "data")`), with groups and annotations from `meta.data`.

```{r seurat, fig.width = 9, fig.alt = "The same genes-as-rows heatmap drawn from a Seurat object holding the simulated data, grouped by cell type."}
library(SeuratObject)
seu <- suppressWarnings(CreateSeuratObject(
  counts = counts(sce),
  meta.data = as.data.frame(colData(sce))
))
seu <- SetAssayData(seu, layer = "data", new.data = logcounts(sce))
heat_map(
  seu,
  features = markers,
  group_by = "cell_type",
  group_max = 100,
  swap_axes = TRUE,
  axis_text_x = NA,
  title = "From a Seurat object"
)
```

### On-disk data

Assays too large for memory can stay on disk. A `SingleCellExperiment` whose assays are `DelayedArray` objects - e.g. written with HDF5Array's `writeHDF5Array()` or `writeTENxMatrix()`, or loaded with `HDF5Array::loadHDF5SummarizedExperiment()` - and a `Seurat` object whose layers are BPCells matrices are read like those in memory: heatmaps and dot plots read only the chosen features of the cells shown, and summaries, markers and scores of every gene read the data a block of genes at a time, each block realised as a sparse (or dense) matrix and passed to the same compiled code, so the results are the same as those of the data in memory. (A `DelayedArray` that only wraps a matrix in memory is read as that matrix.) Here the logs of the counts are left as a delayed operation, which is read in blocks like data on disk:

```{r on-disk}
disk <- sce
assay(disk, "log1p") <- log1p(DelayedArray::DelayedArray(counts(sce)))
class(assay(disk, "log1p"))
memory <- sce
assay(memory, "log1p") <- log1p(counts(sce))
all.equal(
  heat_map_markers(disk, group_by = "cell_type", assay = "log1p"),
  heat_map_markers(memory, group_by = "cell_type", assay = "log1p")
)
```

```{r on-disk-hdf5, eval = FALSE}
# AN HDF5-BACKED OBJECT, SAVED ONCE AND LOADED WITHOUT READING THE COUNTS
HDF5Array::saveHDF5SummarizedExperiment(sce, "pbmc_h5")
disk <- HDF5Array::loadHDF5SummarizedExperiment("pbmc_h5")
heat_map_summarise(disk, group_by = "cell_type")
```

A block holds 2^24 values of all the cells (128 MB as a dense matrix) or eight times as many values of sparse data; `options(HeatmapR.block_values = )` sets the size.

## Summaries of groups

`heat_map_summarise()` reduces the cells of each group to one row: the mean, median, sum, number or proportion detected, or any function, of each feature. For sparse data the mean, sum, number, proportion detected and median are found from the non-zero values in compiled code, without a dense copy of the data, and equal those of the dense data exactly.

```{r summarise, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the mean log-normalised expression of 24 marker genes in each of the six cell types, scaled within each gene, with the cell types and genes clustered by dendrograms."}
means <- heat_map_summarise(sce, features = unlist(markers), group_by = "cell_type")
dense <- heat_map_summarise(
  as.matrix(Matrix::t(logcounts(sce)[unlist(markers), ])),
  group_y = sce$cell_type
)
# THE SAME NUMBERS ([, ] DROPS THE NUMBER OF CELLS IN EACH GROUP, WHICH THE
# SUMMARY OF group_by ALSO KEEPS)
identical(means[, ], dense)
heat_map(means, scale = "column", tree = "both",
         title = "Mean expression of each cell type")
```

## Markers

`heat_map_markers()` scores every feature in every group by its AUC against all the other cells: the chance that a cell of the group has the larger value, ties counting half (the Wilcoxon rank-sum statistic, Wilcoxon 1945 and Mann and Whitney 1947, over the product of the numbers of cells, as presto's `wilcoxauc()` scores markers; Korsunsky et al. 2019). Features are kept for a group when they are detected in at least `min_detected` (0.1) of its cells and their mean is at least `min_logfc` (0.25) above the other cells'; each feature marks the group where its AUC is highest, and the top `n` of each group are flagged in the `top` column. Only features that pass the filters are ranked, and the zeros of sparse data share one rank, so only the non-zero values are sorted. Each AUC comes with the p-value of the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (`p_value`, as `wilcox.test(exact = FALSE)` finds it) and its false discovery rate within the group (`p_adj`, by the method of Benjamini and Hochberg 1995, adjusted over every gene scored). With thousands of cells nearly every marker has a tiny p-value, so the AUC and the difference of the means say more about how well a gene marks a group.

```{r markers}
m <- heat_map_markers(sce, group_by = "cell_type", n = 3)
head(m[m$top, ], 8)
attr(m, "features")
```

The markers can be given to `features`: the rows with `top = TRUE` are shown, the columns grouped and labelled by the group they mark (as scanpy's `var_group_positions` brackets do). Edit `top` to choose other markers.

```{r markers-heatmap, fig.alt = "Heatmap of at most 150 cells of each cell type by the three top markers of each type found by heat_map_markers, the genes grouped and labelled by the cell type they mark and the cells grouped by cell type, giving a block diagonal of high values."}
heat_map(
  sce,
  features = m,
  group_by = "cell_type",
  group_max = 150,
  axis_text_y = NA,
  title = "Top markers of each cell type"
)
```

## Dot plots

`heat_map_dot()` draws one row per group and one column per feature: the colour of each dot is the group's mean scaled within the feature (z-scores clipped at ±2.5, as Seurat's `DotPlot()` (Hao et al. 2024), by default; `scale = "range"` for scanpy's 0 to 1 (Wolf, Angerer and Theis 2018)), and its area the proportion of the group's cells in which the feature is detected, with a size legend in percent.

```{r dot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Dot plot of the three top markers of each of six cell types: one row per cell type and one column per gene, grouped and labelled by the cell type each gene marks. Large dark red dots on the diagonal show each type's markers expressed in most of its cells; elsewhere the dots are small and blue."}
heat_map_dot(sce, features = m, group_by = "cell_type", title = "Top markers")
```

Every `heat_map()` setting can be added, e.g. a dendrogram of the groups and scanpy's scaling:

```{r dot-range, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4.5, fig.alt = "Dot plot of the same markers with the means scaled from 0 to 1 within each gene and a dendrogram of the cell types on the left, which places related types such as CD4 and CD8 T cells next to each other."}
heat_map_dot(sce, features = m, group_by = "cell_type", scale = "range",
             tree_y = TRUE, dot_min = 0.05, title = "Scaled 0 to 1")
```

The markers themselves can be drawn as a dot plot: `heat_map_dot(m)` colours each dot by the log fold change of the gene in the group and sizes it by -log10 of the adjusted p-value (as scanpy's `rank_genes_groups_dotplot()`), with `marker_colour` and `marker_size` for other columns (e.g. `"auc"` or `"detected_in"`). A gene has a dot in each group where it passed the filters of `heat_map_markers()`; with `min_detected = 0` and `min_logfc = -Inf` every gene passes in every group, so the dot plot also shows where each marker is lower than in the other cells:

```{r dot-markers, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Dot plot of the three top markers of each of six cell types, coloured by log fold change and sized by minus log10 of the adjusted p-value. Each type's markers are large red dots in its row, and the same genes are small light blue dots in the other rows, lower there than in the other cells."}
all_pairs <- heat_map_markers(sce, group_by = "cell_type", n = 3,
                              min_detected = 0, min_logfc = -Inf)
heat_map_dot(all_pairs, title = "Markers by fold change and p-value")
```

### Groups within groups

Several columns in `group_by` group the cells by their combinations, ordered by the first column and then the next within it. A dot plot then has one row per combination, grouped by the first column in labelled strips and labelled by the others, so conditions can be compared within each cell type:

```{r dot-condition, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6.5, fig.alt = "Dot plot of the three top markers of each cell type with two rows per cell type, control and treated, grouped in labelled strips by cell type. The markers of each type are large dark red dots in both of its rows."}
heat_map_dot(sce, features = m, group_by = c("cell_type", "condition"),
             title = "Markers in each condition")
```

`split_by` shows two conditions in one row instead, each dot split down the middle (see the cytometry example below).

`heat_map()` splits and labels the cells of each combination (`group_max` then takes that many cells from each), and `heat_map_summarise()` gives one row per combination, e.g. a pseudobulk of the counts of each cell type in each donor:

```{r pseudobulk}
pseudobulk <- heat_map_summarise(sce, features = unlist(markers), assay = "counts",
                                 group_by = c("cell_type", "sample"), fun = "sum")
dim(pseudobulk)
head(rownames(pseudobulk))
```

## Gene-set scores

`heat_map_score()` scores each cell for each of several sets of genes, so a heatmap or dot plot can show a handful of pathways or programs in place of hundreds of genes. `method = "zscore"` (the default) averages the genes of a set after z-scoring each across the cells, so a highly expressed gene doesn't outweigh the others; `"mean"` averages the values themselves; and `"module"` subtracts the mean of control genes of similar expression (the score of Tirosh et al. 2016, as Seurat's `AddModuleScore()` computes it): every gene is binned by its mean expression and, for each gene of the set, 100 genes of its bin are drawn as controls with a fixed seed, so a score above zero means more expression than genes of that level usually have. The scores are computed from the non-zero values of sparse data, and come back as one column per set with the metadata of the cells, so they are drawn and summarised like genes:

```{r scores, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Dot plot of four module scores, T, B, myeloid and NK, in six cell types. Each score is a large dark red dot in the cell types of its program, and small blue dots elsewhere."}
programs <- list(
  T = c("CD3E", "IL7R", "CD8A", "CD8B"),
  B = c("MS4A1", "CD79A", "CD79B", "BANK1"),
  Myeloid = c("LYZ", "S100A8", "S100A9", "FCER1A", "CST3"),
  NK = c("GNLY", "NKG7", "PRF1", "GZMB")
)
scores <- heat_map_score(sce, programs, method = "module")
head(scores)
heat_map_dot(scores, group_by = "cell_type", title = "Module scores")
```

In the dot plot the size of each dot is the share of the group's cells scoring above zero (`threshold`). The markers of `heat_map_markers()` give one set per group (`heat_map_score(sce, m)`), and sets naming genes that aren't in the data are scored on the genes that are, with a message.

### Aligned data sets

`heat_map_align()` draws data sets measured on the same cells or groups side by side - genes and surface proteins (ADT) of CITE-seq, expression and chromatin accessibility, or genes and scores - as blocks of one heatmap. The rows are matched by name and put in one order, clustered (`tree = TRUE`) or split by k-means (`tree_kmeans`) on the `main` data set alone; each block is scaled on its own and has its own colour scale and legend, so values in different units never share a scale. The mean marker genes of each cell type beside their module scores, the genes z-scored within each gene and the scores on a diverging scale centred at zero:

```{r align, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Two heatmap blocks side by side for six cell types: the mean expression of 24 marker genes, z-scored within each gene, and four module scores on a blue to red scale centred at zero. The rows are clustered on the genes, and each block has its own colour legend. Each cell type is high for its own four marker genes and for its own program's score."}
program_means <- heat_map_summarise(scores, group_by = "cell_type")
heat_map_align(
  list(Genes = means, Programs = program_means),
  scale = list("column", NULL),
  cell_col_scale = list(NULL, "Blue-Red 3"),
  cell_col_scale_center = list(NULL, 0),
  tree = TRUE,
  title = "Marker genes and module scores of each cell type"
)
```

With `axis = "y"` data sets that share their columns (e.g. genes and proteins as rows, groups as columns) are stacked as blocks of rows. `heat_map(cell_col_blocks_x = )` gives any heatmap blocks of columns on their own colour scales.

## Cytometry

Cytometry data arrive with events as rows and markers as columns. A matrix or data frame works as it is, with `group_by` and `annotation_by` naming its columns (which are then left out of the features); `flowFrame` and `flowSet` objects are read directly, without flowCore, with markers named by their description (e.g. `"CD3"`) or channel (`"FL1-A"`), and a flowSet's samples and phenotype data as metadata:

```{r flow, eval = FALSE}
heat_map_summarise(fs, features = c("CD3", "CD4", "CD8"), group_by = "cluster",
                   fun = "median")
heat_map(fs, features = c("CD3", "CD4", "CD8"), group_by = "cluster",
         group_max = 500, annotation_by = "sample")
```

Mass cytometry intensities are usually transformed with asinh(x / 5) (Bendall et al. 2011) (a cofactor of about 150 for flow cytometry) and each marker then scaled from 0 to 1 between its 1st and 99th percentiles, so that a few bright events don't compress the colours of all the others. `heat_map_summarise()` does both: `transform = "asinh"` with `cofactor`, and `scale = "quantile"` with `q`, applied to the medians of the clusters (`scale_when = "last"`, the default) or to the events before summarising them (`"first"`).

Below, `heat_map_example("cytometry")`: 200,000 simulated events with 12 markers in eight clusters, from eight samples in two conditions, as raw intensities. Cluster C3 is twice as common in the stimulated samples, and HLA-DR rises in clusters C5 and C6 under stimulation.

```{r cytometry-data}
events <- heat_map_example("cytometry")
markers <- names(events)[1:12]
markers
head(events, 3)
```

The medians of each cluster, with `stack_by` counting the events of each condition in each cluster. The summary keeps the number of events in each cluster and in each part of it (its `"n"` and `"stack"` attributes), which `bar_values_y = "n"` draws as bars beside the clusters, stacked by condition with `bar_type_y = "stack"` (`"fill"` draws the proportions instead):

```{r cytometry, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the median of 12 markers in eight clusters of 200,000 simulated cytometry events, asinh-transformed and scaled from 0 to 1 within each marker, with dendrograms of the clusters and markers and, beside the clusters, bars of their numbers of events split into control and stimulated."}
medians <- heat_map_summarise(
  events,
  features = markers,
  group_by = "cluster",
  fun = "median",
  transform = "asinh",
  cofactor = 5,
  scale = "quantile",
  q = 0.01,
  stack_by = "condition"
)
attr(medians, "stack")
heat_map(
  medians,
  tree = "both",
  bar_values_y = "n",
  bar_type_y = "stack",
  bar_size_y = 1.6,
  bar_fill_y = c(control = "grey60", stimulated = "#D7191C"),
  legend_title = "Scaled median",
  title = "Median of each cluster"
)
```

The distribution behind each median can be drawn inside its cell, here from 2,000 events of each cluster:

```{r cytometry-values, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the asinh-transformed median of 12 markers in eight clusters, scaled within each marker, with a density of each cluster's values inside every cell."}
sub <- events[heat_map_downsample(events$cluster, 2000), ]
heat_map(
  heat_map_summarise(sub, features = markers, group_by = "cluster",
                     fun = "median", transform = "asinh"),
  scale = "column",
  cell_values = heat_map_summarise(sub, features = markers, group_by = "cluster",
                                   fun = "values", transform = "asinh"),
  tree = "both",
  title = "Distributions behind the medians"
)
```

Grouping by cluster and sample (`group_by = c("cluster", "sample")`) gives the median of each cluster in each sample, the view of differential states. The summary keeps the metadata that is the same for every event of each row, here the sample and its condition (its `"groups"` attribute), so that `heat_map()` can group and annotate its rows by them:

```{r cytometry-states, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 9, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the median of HLA-DR, CD45RA and CCR7 in each of eight clusters in each of eight samples, grouped by cluster with labelled strips and annotated by sample and condition, with bars of the number of events in each row; HLA-DR is higher in the stimulated samples of clusters C5 and C6."}
states <- heat_map_summarise(
  events,
  features = c("HLA-DR", "CD45RA", "CCR7"),
  group_by = c("cluster", "sample"),
  fun = "median",
  transform = "asinh",
  scale = "quantile"
)
head(attr(states, "groups"))
heat_map(
  states,
  group_by = "cluster",
  annotation_by = c("sample", "condition"),
  axis_text_y = NA,
  bar_values_y = "n",
  bar_size_y = 1.6,
  legend_title = "Scaled median",
  title = "Median of each cluster in each sample"
)
```

A dot plot split by condition compares the conditions in each dot: with `split_by = "condition"`, the left half of each dot shows the control events of the cluster and the right half the stimulated, each half coloured by its mean of the asinh-transformed intensities (`transform = "asinh"`, z-scored within each marker across the clusters and both conditions) and sized by the proportion of its events above `threshold`, here asinh 2 as positive:

```{r cytometry-split, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Dot plot of 12 markers in eight clusters with each dot split down the middle, the control events of the cluster in the left half and the stimulated in the right. The halves match except for HLA-DR in clusters C5 and C6, whose right halves are larger and darker red."}
heat_map_dot(events, features = markers, group_by = "cluster",
             split_by = "condition", transform = "asinh", threshold = 2,
             title = "Control (left) and stimulated (right)")
```

## Clusters that may be two populations

A cluster can combine two populations that clustering didn't separate, differing in one or two features. `bimodal = TRUE` outlines the cells of a summary or dot plot in which a group's cells look like two populations, so that such clusters can be looked into. Each outline comes from the dip statistic of Hartigan and Hartigan (1985), the distance between the distribution of a feature's values in the group and the closest distribution with one peak. The dip is 0 for one peak of any shape, about 0.02 for two equal populations 3 standard deviations apart and 0.05 for 4. A cell is outlined when its dip is at least 0.01 and above the dip that one population of as many cells exceeds 1% of the time (0.06 for 100 cells, 0.02 for 1,000), so that small groups aren't outlined by chance.

Peaks can come from the measurement and its transformation rather than from cells: piles of zeros, the two mirrored peaks the asinh transform with too small a cofactor makes of a negative population, the comb of 1, 2, 3, ... counts on a log scale, saturated detectors. So the dips are found from the values above `threshold` (the cells in which a feature is detected, which dot sizes already show), after the transform and before scaling, with discrete values spread over the gaps between them and the piles at the ends of continuous values left out. On simulated data none of these was outlined, while two populations 3 standard deviations apart were in groups of 5,000 cells.

Below, clusters C1 and C2 of the cytometry events are joined, as a clustering at lower resolution might join them. The markers that separate them are outlined in the joined cluster, and the bars show the largest dip of each cluster:

```{r bimodal-cytometry, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 5, fig.alt = "Heatmap of the scaled median of 12 markers in seven clusters, one of them joining clusters C1 and C2, with a density of each cluster's values inside every cell. The cells of the joined cluster in the markers that separate C1 from C2 are outlined with thick borders, their densities showing two peaks, and bars beside the rows show the largest dip of each cluster, by far the largest for the joined cluster."}
joined <- events
joined$cluster[joined$cluster %in% c("C1", "C2")] <- "C1+C2"
medians <- heat_map_summarise(joined, features = markers, group_by = "cluster",
                              fun = "median", transform = "asinh",
                              scale = "quantile", bimodal = TRUE)
sub <- joined[heat_map_downsample(joined$cluster, 2000), ]
heat_map(
  medians,
  bimodal = TRUE,
  cell_values = heat_map_summarise(sub, features = markers,
                                   group_by = "cluster", fun = "values",
                                   transform = "asinh"),
  bar_values_y = "dip",
  legend_title = "Scaled median",
  title = "C1 and C2 joined"
)
round(attr(medians, "dip")["C1+C2", ], 3)
```

Populations that differ in whether features are detected at all, such as CD4 and CD8 T cells in one cluster, each without the other's markers, don't give any single feature two peaks: on the count scale a feature detected in only some of the cells falls away steadily from zero, as dropout does. They are found across features instead, from the dip of the cells' scores on the first principal component of the correlations of the features shown within the cluster, when that component carries real co-variation (an eigenvalue above the upper edge of the Marchenko-Pastur law for independent features; Marchenko and Pastur 1967), so that features with two peaks of their own don't add up to a split, and the features that drive it are outlined. Here the CD4 and CD8 T cells of the blood cells are one cluster:

```{r bimodal-dot, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 4, fig.alt = "Dot plot of four marker genes of each of six cell types in five groups of cells, one of them joining the CD4 and CD8 T cells. The dots of the joined T cells in the CD4 and CD8 T cell markers have thick outlines."}
cells <- as.data.frame(colData(sce))
cells$group <- as.character(cells$cell_type)
cells$group[cells$group %in% c("CD4 T", "CD8 T")] <- "T cells"
hm <- heat_map_dot(sce, features = metadata(sce)$markers, group_by = cells$group,
                   bimodal = TRUE, title = "CD4 and CD8 T cells joined")
```

`heat_map_describe()` names what is outlined, and `heat_map_info(hm)$bimodal` returns the dips:

```{r bimodal-describe}
heat_map_describe(hm)
```

An outline is a prompt to look, not a verdict: the distributions inside the cells (`cell_values`) show what the dip has found, and two states of one population (e.g. stimulated and resting cells) are two peaks too.

## Trajectories

Along a trajectory, genes are smoothed along pseudotime and ordered by when they peak. `heat_map_smooth()` bins the cells along `along` (a pseudotime column, or a vector), with `bins` bins of equal numbers of cells (`binning = "width"` for equal widths), and finds each gene's mean over the `span` bins around each bin. The result has one row per bin and keeps the position of each bin, which `annotation_by` draws as a track; `tree_order_y = "peak"` (with the genes as rows) orders the genes by where they are highest.

Below, `heat_map_example("trajectory")`: 4,000 simulated cells of a branching trajectory, with a pseudotime for each of two lineages as slingshot (Street et al. 2018) gives them (missing for cells outside the lineage). Both lineages share their start and branch at a pseudotime of 0.4, and 30 genes, in a random order, each peak at their own point, some in one lineage only.

```{r trajectory-data}
traj <- heat_map_example("trajectory", class = "SingleCellExperiment")
traj
head(colData(traj))
```

The genes along the pseudotime of all the cells, ordered by when they peak:

```{r trajectory, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Heatmap of 30 genes, one per row, smoothed along pseudotime in 60 bins, one per column, each gene scaled from 0 to 1, with a pseudotime track above. The genes are ordered by when they peak, so their highest values run diagonally from the top left to the bottom right."}
smooth <- heat_map_smooth(traj, along = "pseudotime", bins = 60)
heat_map(
  smooth,
  swap_axes = TRUE,
  scale = "row",
  tree_order_y = "peak",
  annotation_by = "pseudotime",
  axis_text_x = NA,
  title = "Genes along pseudotime"
)
```

Several `along` columns smooth each lineage on its own (`group_by` does the same for one pseudotime and a lineage column), and `group_by = "lineage"` draws the lineages side by side. The peak order reads the position of each bin along the trajectory, so the genes of both lineages are ordered by when they peak:

```{r trajectory-lineages, fig.width = 9, fig.height = 6, fig.alt = "Heatmap of 30 genes smoothed along the pseudotime of two lineages, drawn side by side with labelled strips and a pseudotime track. The genes are ordered by when they peak: genes peaking early are high in both lineages, later genes in lineage 1, lineage 2 or both."}
lineages <- heat_map_smooth(traj, along = c("lineage1", "lineage2"), bins = 40)
head(attr(lineages, "groups"))
heat_map(
  lineages,
  swap_axes = TRUE,
  group_by = "lineage",
  scale = "row",
  tree_order_y = "peak",
  annotation_by = "along",
  axis_text_x = NA,
  title = "Two lineages"
)
```

Without a pseudotime, `tree_order_y = "spectral"` orders the cells themselves along a trajectory; see the [ordering guide](ordering.html).

## Speed

```{r speed-setup, include = FALSE}
sc <- utils::read.csv("single-cell-benchmarks.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sc_info <- readLines("single-cell-benchmarks-info.txt")
sc_info <- stats::setNames(sub("^[^:]*: ", "", sc_info), sub(":.*", "", sc_info))
sc$size <- paste(format(sc$cells, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "cells x",
                 format(sc$genes, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE), "genes")
sc_summary <- function(task) {
  r <- sc[sc$task == task, ]
  key <- paste(r$method, r$size, sep = "\r")
  out <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(r, factor(key, levels = unique(key))), function(z) {
    ok <- z$status == "ok"
    data.frame(method = z$method[1], size = z$size[1],
               n = as.numeric(z$cells[1]) * z$genes[1],
               seconds = if(any(ok)) stats::median(z$seconds[ok]) else NA,
               peak_mb = if(any(ok)) max(z$peak_mb[ok]) else NA,
               status = if(any(ok)) "ok" else z$status[1])
  }))
  rownames(out) <- NULL
  out
}
sc_table <- function(task, value = c("time", "memory"), caption = NULL) {
  value <- match.arg(value)
  s <- sc_summary(task)
  sizes <- unique(s$size[order(s$n)])
  methods <- unique(s$method)
  tab <- sapply(methods, function(m) {
    z <- s[s$method == m, ][match(sizes, s$size[s$method == m]), ]
    v <- if(value == "time") {
      ifelse(z$status == "ok",
             ifelse(z$seconds < 10, sprintf("%.2f", z$seconds), sprintf("%.0f", z$seconds)),
             z$status)
    } else {
      ifelse(z$status != "ok", z$status,
             ifelse(z$peak_mb < 0.5, "< 1", format(round(z$peak_mb), big.mark = ",")))
    }
    v[is.na(z$method)] <- ""
    v
  })
  tab <- matrix(tab, nrow = length(sizes), dimnames = list(sizes, methods))
  knitr::kable(tab, align = "r", caption = caption)
}
# THE RANGE OF THE RATIOS OF THE TIMES OF TWO METHODS OVER THE SIZES
sum_ratio <- function(a, b, task = "summarise") {
  s <- sc_summary(task)
  sa <- s[s$method == a, ]
  r <- sa$seconds / s$seconds[s$method == b][match(sa$size, s$size[s$method == b])]
  paste(sprintf("%.1f", range(r)), collapse = " to ")
}
sc_get <- function(task, method, size, value = "seconds") {
  s <- sc_summary(task)
  s[[value]][s$method == method & s$size == size][1]
}
```

The single-cell functions were timed against their counterparts in Seurat `r sc_info[["Seurat"]]`, scran `r sc_info[["scran"]]` and scuttle `r sc_info[["scuttle"]]` on simulated counts of 12 cell types (10 marker genes each, about 10% of the other genes' values non-zero), log-normalised and held as sparse matrices with genes as rows, as each package stores them. Each case ran in a fresh R process on the machine of the [speed comparison](benchmarks.html) (`r sc_info[["cores"]]` cores, `r sc_info[["memory_gb"]]` GB), three times when it took less than 30 seconds, and the median is shown; runs were stopped after 10 minutes. Memory is the growth of the process's resident memory during the run, with the data already loaded.

In short:

- **Markers.** `heat_map_markers()` ranked the markers of 12 groups in 20,000 cells and 20,000 genes in `r round(sc_get("markers", "HeatmapR", "20,000 cells x 20,000 genes"), 2)` seconds, where scran took `r round(sc_get("markers", "scran (scoreMarkers)", "20,000 cells x 20,000 genes"))` to `r round(sc_get("markers", "scran", "20,000 cells x 20,000 genes"))` seconds and Seurat `r round(sc_get("markers", "Seurat", "20,000 cells x 20,000 genes"))` seconds and `r format(round(sc_get("markers", "Seurat", "20,000 cells x 20,000 genes", "peak_mb") / 1000, 1))` GB. Like Seurat, HeatmapR scores only the features that pass its filters, one group against the rest; scran's functions compute statistics for every gene between every pair of groups, which takes longer and tells you more.
- **Summaries.** scuttle's `summarizeAssayByGroup()` was the fastest at the mean and proportion detected of every gene, `r sum_ratio("HeatmapR", "scuttle")` times as fast as `heat_map_summarise()` (which makes one pass for each), and Seurat's `AverageExpression()` took `r sum_ratio("Seurat", "HeatmapR")` times as long as HeatmapR, with up to `r format(round(max(sc_summary("summarise")$peak_mb[sc_summary("summarise")$method == "Seurat"]) / 1000, 1))` GB of memory. For a heatmap or dot plot only the chosen features are summarised.
- **Plots.** A dot plot of 40 genes in 100,000 cells took `r round(sc_get("dotplot", "HeatmapR", "100,000 cells x 2,000 genes"), 2)` seconds against `r round(sc_get("dotplot", "Seurat", "100,000 cells x 2,000 genes"), 1)` for Seurat's `DotPlot()`, and a heatmap of the 40 genes in every one of the 100,000 cells `r round(sc_get("heatmap", "HeatmapR", "100,000 cells x 2,000 genes"), 1)` seconds against `r round(sc_get("heatmap", "Seurat", "100,000 cells x 2,000 genes"))` seconds and `r format(round(sc_get("heatmap", "Seurat", "100,000 cells x 2,000 genes", "peak_mb") / 1000, 1))` GB for `DoHeatmap()`.

**Markers of every group against the other cells**: `heat_map_markers(sce, group_by = "group")`, scran's `scoreMarkers()` (AUCs and other effect sizes between every pair of groups) and `findMarkers(test.type = "wilcox", direction = "up")` (Wilcoxon tests between every pair of groups), and Seurat's `FindAllMarkers(only.pos = TRUE, min.pct = 0.1, logfc.threshold = 0.25)` (one-vs-rest Wilcoxon tests`r if(sc_info[["presto"]] == "FALSE") ", without the presto package, which Seurat uses to speed them up when it is installed"`). Times in seconds:

```{r speed-markers, echo = FALSE}
sc_table("markers")
```

Peak memory in MB:

```{r speed-markers-memory, echo = FALSE}
sc_table("markers", "memory")
```

**Mean and proportion detected of every gene in every group** (pseudobulk): `heat_map_summarise()` (twice, once for each), scuttle's `summarizeAssayByGroup(statistics = c("mean", "prop.detected"))` and Seurat's `AverageExpression()`. Times in seconds:

```{r speed-summarise, echo = FALSE}
sc_table("summarise")
```

**A dot plot of 40 genes** (`heat_map_dot()` and Seurat's `DotPlot()`) and **a heatmap of 40 genes in every cell**, grouped (`heat_map(swap_axes = TRUE)` and Seurat's `DoHeatmap()`), drawn to a PNG file. Times in seconds:

```{r speed-plots, echo = FALSE}
sc_table("dotplot", caption = "Dot plot")
sc_table("heatmap", caption = "Heatmap")
```

Peak memory of the heatmaps in MB:

```{r speed-heatmap-memory, echo = FALSE}
sc_table("heatmap", "memory")
```

The scripts are in [`data-raw/benchmarks`](https://github.com/DillonHammill/HeatmapR/tree/master/data-raw/benchmarks): `single-cell-case.R` runs one case and `single-cell-run.R` runs them all and writes `vignettes/articles/single-cell-benchmarks.csv`, which this page reads.
